transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I came in because things are just... they're really starting to mess with my work and my social life. I just can't stop focusing on how uneven and puffy the left side of my face looks. It's really obvious on video calls. I'm a computer support specialist, so I'm on camera all day helping people. We actually just switched our whole company over to a new software system last month, which has been a total nightmare because nobody reads the training manuals I write. I spent like three weeks just walking people through the exact same audio settings over and over. 

But anyway, whenever I'm on those calls, I just stare at how lopsided my face is. And it ruins my salsa photos, too. I've been taking salsa classes at this place downtown—it's right above this amazing bakery, so when we finish at night the whole street smells like fresh sourdough, it's honestly the best part of the week. But the studio posts pictures online, and I just zero in on my face and how puffy that left side is in every single shot. Everyone keeps telling me they don't see anything at all, which makes no sense to me, but... yeah, it's just getting to be too much.
Do you find yourself doing anything repeatedly—like checking mirrors, touching your face, or adjusting your appearance—because of how you feel about the left side of your face?

Yeah, um, especially before my meetings or if I'm trying to go out somewhere. I'll just sit there opening and closing the camera preview. Which, honestly, the new webcams work gave us are just awful. They bought these cheap clip-on ones because accounting wouldn't approve the budget for the ones with the built-in ring lights. My manager, Dave, was supposed to fight for them, but he just folded immediately. He always does that, just agrees with whatever the finance team says. It's so frustrating because those cheap lenses distort everything and the color balance is completely off. 

But anyway, I'll sit there changing the angle, moving my desk lamp around, and trying to fix my hair so it falls right over that side of my face to hide it. My hair is kind of tricky to style anyway. I have this friend Sarah from my salsa class who has this perfect, bouncy curly hair that never frizzes, even when it's super humid. We went out for tacos last week and it was pouring rain, and her hair still looked like a literal shampoo commercial. I really wish my hair did that, it would be so much easier. 

But yeah, I end up fixing my hair, retaking pictures of myself over and over, and just constantly texting my friends asking if I look weird or if the puffiness is super obvious. I just keep asking them and checking the camera until... well, usually until I'm totally late for whatever I'm supposed to be doing, or I just get so completely drained from the whole routine that I don't even have the energy to go out anymore.

Do these concerns about the way your face looks interfere with your ability to function normally, such as causing you to avoid social situations, feel extremely anxious during video calls, or have trouble concentrating on your work?

Yeah, it definitely does... I mean, I've actually missed some of my IT ticket deadlines because of it. And I've joined some video calls late because I just couldn't get past how my face looked in the camera preview. It actually got so bad that my supervisor brought it up in my last performance review. Which was incredibly awkward. Dave scheduled the review on a Friday afternoon, which is just the absolute worst time because everyone is trying to log off for the weekend, and they ordered these stale turkey sandwiches for the conference room. I don't know why corporate can't just cater from the deli down the street, their pastrami is amazing and it's literally a block away. I swear the finance team just looks for the cheapest catering option on Google and clicks the first link. 

But anyway, yeah, he noticed I was logging into meetings late. And outside of work... it's affecting that too. I've skipped a bunch of salsa nights recently, and some of the community events downtown. There was this huge street fair last weekend with all these local artisans and this amazing French crepe truck. I love crepes, especially the ones with Nutella and strawberries, my roommate in grad school used to make them from scratch on Sundays. But I knew everyone from the neighborhood would be taking photos and tagging them online. I just couldn't handle the thought of it, so I stayed home. I basically just skip all those things now when I know people will be taking pictures.
Have you been feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in activities you used to enjoy, even outside of concerns about your appearance?

I mean, not really? Like, I don't think I'm depressed or anything. I still want to do things, I still want to go to salsa and hang out with my friends. It's just the picture thing that stops me. If I knew nobody was going to take photos, I'd be out there every night. Actually, speaking of going out, my friend Sarah—the one with the perfect hair—she's been trying to get me to join this indoor rock climbing gym with her. She says it's a great workout and the community is super supportive. I guess they have these beginner nights where they teach you how to tie the knots and belay and everything. It sounds kind of fun, but the chalk... I don't know, I feel like the chalk dust would get everywhere, and I have this really nice black Patagonia fleece that I wear all the time because it's always freezing in my apartment. My landlord controls the thermostat for the whole building, which I'm pretty sure is illegal, or at least super annoying. I've sent him like three emails about it, and he always just says 'I'll look into it,' but he never does. 

But anyway, yeah, I still have interest in doing stuff. I don't feel hopeless or anything like that. It's really just the stress about my face that gets in the way of actually doing the things I want to do.
Do you ever feel intense anxiety or distress specifically about the way your face looks, even when you know others don’t notice anything wrong?

Yeah, I definitely get super anxious about it. It's like this overwhelming panic sometimes. Even when my friends tell me I look completely fine or that they literally can't see what I'm talking about, it doesn't help at all. I know they're probably just trying to be nice, honestly. People do that, you know? Like when my mom tells me she loves this one green sweater I wear. It's this hideous pea-green color that I bought on sale at Old Navy like five years ago, and the sleeves are slightly too short, but she always says it brings out my eyes. Moms just say stuff like that to make you feel good. Which reminds me, I really need to call her. She's been trying to figure out how to set up her new smart TV, and she keeps texting me these blurry photos of the remote control asking which button is for Netflix. I tried explaining it over the phone, but she just gets so frustrated with technology. 

But yeah, even if people say they don't notice the puffiness or whatever, I still feel incredibly distressed about it. It just gnaws at me, and I can't stop thinking about how obvious it must be to everyone else.

Do you believe that the puffiness or unevenness on the left side of your face is a real, physical problem that others should be able to see, or is it more of a feeling that something is wrong even if others don’t notice it?

I mean... I don't really know how to answer that. Like, I'm not sure? I definitely see it, so to me it feels like a real, physical thing, but I don't know if it's just a feeling or what. I mostly notice it when I'm looking at my webcam. 

Actually, I just bought this new 4K webcam from Logitech because the one built into my Dell work laptop is absolute garbage. It literally makes everyone look like a pixelated potato. I thought maybe a better camera would help, so I ordered one on Amazon with this whole ring light attachment. But the delivery was a complete nightmare. The driver left it at the wrong apartment building—he left it at building 4 instead of 40, which happens all the time because the numbers on our buildings are painted in this really weird, modern font that's impossible to read from the street. My neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, she actually petitioned the HOA to get them changed, but the board president is this guy Steve who thinks he's some kind of architectural genius. He completely refused. He's the same guy who tried to ban window AC units last summer, which is ridiculous because the central air here barely works and it gets so humid in August. 

But um... what were you asking? Oh, right, if it's a real problem or just a feeling. Yeah, I honestly don't know how to categorize it. I just know that I see it and it really bothers me.
Do you ever try to mentally 'fix' the way your face looks in your head, or do anything in your mind over and over—like analyzing how bad it looks or imagining how it could be different?

I mean, I don't know if I do it in my head so much, but I definitely do things over and over before I have to be seen. Like, before a meeting or if I'm supposed to go out, I'll just sit there and keep opening the camera preview. And I'll change the angle, move the lighting around, try to fix my hair so it covers that side of my face better. I'll take a bunch of pictures to see how it looks, and then I usually end up texting my friends to ask if I look strange or if the puffiness is super obvious. 

Which, speaking of my hair, I really need to find a new stylist. The girl I usually go to, Becca, she just moved to Austin. Everyone is moving to Austin right now, I swear. It's like the new tech hub or whatever. My cousin actually got a job down there working for some startup that makes an app for tracking your dog's bowel movements. It sounds ridiculous, but apparently they got like five million in seed funding. People will spend so much money on their pets. I wanted a dog for a while, maybe a French bulldog, but they have so many health problems. My coworker has one and he spent like four thousand dollars on its nasal surgery because it couldn't breathe. 

But anyway, yeah, I just keep doing the camera thing and asking my friends over and over. I do it so much that half the time I end up being late, or I just feel so completely drained by the whole process that I don't even want to go out anymore.
Do thoughts about the left side of your face being uneven or puffy occupy a lot of your time or attention, even when you're not in front of a camera or about to go out?

Yeah, it's pretty much all I think about. That's honestly why I came in to see you. I just can't stop focusing on how uneven and puffy the left side of my face looks. It's not just the video calls for work, it's also in pictures... like, I do salsa dancing, and whenever someone posts photos from the social nights, I just zero in on my face and it looks so awful. 

Salsa is usually so much fun, though. I go to this place downtown on Thursday nights. They have a live band once a month, which is great, but the floor gets so sticky because people spill their drinks. Last week, this guy spilled half a margarita right where we were dancing. He didn't even apologize, just kept doing his basic step like nothing happened. He was wearing these really intense, shiny dance shoes, too. I don't know why guys think those look good. They remind me of bowling shoes, honestly. Speaking of bowling, my company is doing this team-building bowling night next Friday, and I'm dreading it. Not because of the bowling—I actually have a pretty decent hook—but because I know people are going to be taking pictures for the company newsletter. 

But yeah, the face thing. Everyone keeps telling me they don't see anything wrong, but it's constantly on my mind. It's getting to the point where it's really starting to mess with my work and my social life because I'm just so distracted by it all the time.
Do these thoughts about your face being uneven or puffy cause you significant distress, even when you're not actively looking at yourself or expecting to be photographed?

I mean, I don't really know how to measure "significant distress" or if I'd call it exactly that. I'm not sure. It just... it makes me feel really down, you know? Like, I'll just be sitting there trying to relax, not even near a mirror or a camera, and I just feel this heavy pit in my stomach about how I look. 

I was trying to read a book on the couch yesterday just to take my mind off things, mostly because my eyes get so dry from staring at screens all day. Working in IT support, I'm literally glaring at a monitor for ten hours a day helping people reset their passwords. You wouldn't believe how many people lock themselves out of their accounts on a Monday morning. It's like they completely forget their own names over the weekend. We have this one guy in accounting, Todd, who locked himself out three times in one day last week. Three times! And he always blames the system, saying his keyboard is broken or the network is glitching. I actually had to go down to his cubicle and watch him type his password in, and he was literally just leaving the Caps Lock on. It's so exhausting trying to explain basic computer skills to people who make twice my salary and have these fancy window offices. They get these really nice ergonomic chairs, too—the Herman Miller ones—while we just get the standard issue squeaky mesh ones down in the IT department. 

But um... yeah, I guess I'm not sure if it's the right word for it, but the thoughts definitely ruin my mood and make me feel awful, even when I'm just trying to have a quiet night in by myself.

doctor.question: Do these thoughts about your face being uneven or puffy cause you significant distress, even when you're not actively looking at yourself or expecting to be photographed?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about significant distress caused by the thoughts about the face. While my profile covers Functional Impairment (missing deadlines, skipping events), it does not explicitly cover 'distress' (e.g., feelings of anxiety, sadness, or emotional pain) independent of the functional impairment or preoccupation.

patient.answer:
I mean, I don't really know how to measure "significant distress" or if I'd call it exactly that. I'm not sure. It just... it makes me feel really down, you know? Like, I'll just be sitting there trying to relax, not even near a mirror or a camera, and I just feel this heavy pit in my stomach about how I look. 

I was trying to read a book on the couch yesterday just to take my mind off things, mostly because my eyes get so dry from staring at screens all day. Working in IT support, I'm literally glaring at a monitor for ten hours a day helping people reset their passwords. You wouldn't believe how many people lock themselves out of their accounts on a Monday morning. It's like they completely forget their own names over the weekend. We have this one guy in accounting, Todd, who locked himself out three times in one day last week. Three times! And he always blames the system, saying his keyboard is broken or the network is glitching. I actually had to go down to his cubicle and watch him type his password in, and he was literally just leaving the Caps Lock on. It's so exhausting trying to explain basic computer skills to people who make twice my salary and have these fancy window offices. They get these really nice ergonomic chairs, too—the Herman Miller ones—while we just get the standard issue squeaky mesh ones down in the IT department. 

But um... yeah, I guess I'm not sure if it's the right word for it, but the thoughts definitely ruin my mood and make me feel awful, even when I'm just trying to have a quiet night in by myself.

inference.note: The patient's concerns about facial appearance, specifically preoccupation with perceived facial asymmetry and puffiness, along with repetitive behaviors (checking camera, adjusting appearance, seeking reassurance), significant distress, and impairment in social and occupational functioning, strongly indicate Body Dysmorphic Disorder (F45.22). Depression (F32.9, F33.9) is ruled out as the patient denies depressed mood, hopelessness, or loss of interest, and symptoms are specifically tied to appearance concerns rather than a general low mood.

opening_question.intent: Establish the patient's primary concern or reason for seeking help
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent preoccupation with an imagined or slight defect in appearance (dysmorphophobia), engaging in repetitive behaviors (checking appearance, camouflaging, reassurance seeking), and experiencing significant distress and functional impairment. This aligns with the criteria for body dysmorphic disorder. No sufficient evidence was found for major depressive disorder or specific phobia as primary diagnoses.
